input: Amine absorption is widely regarded as a key technology for capturing carbon dioxide from industrial gas streams, and pilot-scale testing plays a vital role in building confidence before any move to full-scale deployment. In the work described here, an amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln, a source whose gas composition and dust burden make it a demanding application for solvent-based capture. Over a period of 90 days, the unit treated gas at a rate of 13 t of carbon dioxide per day, and it is noteworthy that it captured 92% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas, highlighting the effectiveness of the process under the conditions studied. In addition, the steam demand associated with the process was 3.8 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, while the solvent loss was 1.8 kg per tonne captured. Both figures are important considerations in their own right, because the energy required to regenerate the solvent and the rate at which solvent must be made up feed directly into the operating cost of any capture plant built on this basis. It should be noted, however, that beyond 90 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent remains untested, underscoring the need for further long-term investigation before the results are extrapolated to extended campaigns.
target: An amine absorption unit at pilot scale treated gas from a cement kiln. Over 90 days at 13 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 92% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Kiln gas is the application as well as the test medium: capture and both demands were measured on the gas the process would actually treat, so the figures are not transferred from a cleaner or simpler stream. Steam demand was 3.8 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, and solvent loss was 1.8 kg per tonne captured. Steam demand is the regeneration energy per tonne of product and is the largest single energy input to an amine unit, so the figure sets the energy cost of the process as run. Solvent loss sets the make-up rate, a continuing cost per tonne captured for as long as the unit operates. The capture figure and both demands hold for the test as run, on kiln gas of the composition treated during the test. Beyond 90 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested. Performance over longer campaigns, with dust accumulating in the solvent over time, is not established by this test, and neither is the solvent life that a commercial unit would plan against. A longer test, run with the dust burden present throughout, is the measurement that would settle both questions.
